summary: This RFC describes how the CONVERT IMAP extension can be used in the Sieve mail filtering language to transform messages before final delivery.

eli5.summary: A mail filter that can also change a message into another form, like shrinking a picture, before putting it in your inbox.

questions: what is the sieve convert extension
how to convert attachments in sieve
subtitle: A Sieve action and test that converts message attachments, such as shrinking images, before delivery.

tldr.problem: Sieve mail filters could sort and redirect messages but had no way to transform body parts, such as converting an image to a smaller format, before final delivery.
tldr.mechanism: A new "convert" action converts body parts of one media type to another using the conversion parameters of the IMAP CONVERT extension, and it can also be used as a test that is false if any conversion failed.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can convert attachments before filing, redirecting or keeping a message. A failed conversion leaves the message unchanged and raises no error.

facts.label: On failure
facts.value: Message left unchanged, no error raised

today: RFC 6558 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IMAP CONVERT extension (RFC 5259) adds an IMAP command for client-controlled conversions of whole messages or their body parts. RFC 6558 defines a similar extension for the Sieve mail filtering language (RFC 5228), reusing the conversion parameters and framework established by IMAP CONVERT.

The extension is named convert and a script must list it in its require line.
sections.eli5: Email apps already had a way to ask for a picture to be changed into another kind. This lets a mail filter do the same thing on its own.

sections.title: The convert Action
sections.content:
The usage is convert <from-media-type> <to-media-type> <transcoding-params>. Every body part whose media type (RFC 2046, sometimes called MIME type) equals the first argument is converted to the second, using parameters written as name=value strings as defined in RFC 5259. Messages with no matching body part are not affected.

Outside a foreverypart loop (from the MIME part tests of RFC 5703) the conversion applies equally to all matching body parts. Inside such a loop it applies only to the body part being processed.

A single convert applies only once to any body part. Converting a JPEG to a smaller JPEG does not make the action see a new JPEG to process again.

If a conversion cannot be completed, the action MUST terminate and leave the message unchanged, rolling back any other conversions done by that action. Script processing continues, no error is raised, and no partial conversions from one action are allowed.

Conversions can put a significant load on the server, and computationally expensive conversions of many body parts can be an attack vector. Servers MAY refuse conversions or do them at lower priority. Implementations might also defer a conversion until its result is needed, for example skipping it if a discard follows.
sections.eli5: You say which kind of file to look for and what kind to turn it into. If the change fails, the original is left exactly as it was.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Actions and as a Test
sections.content:
A successful convert effectively changes the message, and all later actions and tests, including other convert actions, see the changed message. Conversions are cumulative. All conversions are done before the implicit keep.

When a disposition-type action such as fileinto or redirect is reached, the message state is locked in for that action. It MUST NOT include conversions that come later in the script. So the sequence convert, fileinto, convert, fileinto stores two different versions: the first uses only the first conversion, the second uses both.

convert can also be used as a test. It attempts the requested conversions and evaluates to false if and only if at least one conversion failed, whether because it was unsupported or because the data could not be converted. This creates a new type of Sieve action, a testable action, and does not make other actions usable as tests.
sections.eli5: Each time the sorter files a copy, it files the message as it looks at that moment. Later changes only show up in later copies.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Example 1 converts all image/tiff parts to image/jpeg with pix-x=320 and pix-y=240, and the converted message gets the implicit keep.

Example 2 wraps the conversion in an if test and files the message into INBOX.pics only if the conversion succeeded. Messages with no TIFF parts are not converted and are kept as usual.

Example 3 uses foreverypart to convert only inline TIFF parts, using 640x480 for parts larger than 500 kilobytes and 320x240 for smaller ones.

Example 4 shows tricky interactions. TIFF parts are converted to 640x480 JPEGs and the message filed; inline JPEGs are then reconverted to 320x240; a message with a Mobile-Link header is redirected with both conversions; and a later test for TIFF parts never matches because the first block already converted them.
sections.eli5: The examples show a few recipes, like shrinking pictures, filing only if it worked, and what happens when several steps follow each other.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of IMAP CONVERT and Sieve apply, and combining the two adds none. The cost of expensive conversions is discussed with the action itself.

IANA added a convert entry to the Sieve Extensions registry, described as adding a new Sieve test and action that enable scripts to perform data conversions on the message being delivered.
sections.eli5: It is as safe as the two things it combines, but heavy conversion work can slow a server, so servers may say no.
